title: Capstone: End-to-End Optimization
blurb: Tests the profile, fix, re-measure loop, ranking stages before fixing them, which chapter's fix applies to each stage, why batching gave the biggest win, the cold-start GPU trap one more time, and what nsys showed about many small GPU calls.

questions.prompt: What is the first step of any "this pipeline is too slow" investigation, per Procedure 57.1?
options: Add more CPU cores and see whether it scales
Profile it and rank stages before changing any code
Rewrite the stage that looks most complex in the source
Move the slowest-looking stage to the GPU
questions.explanation: The real bottleneck often isn't the stage that looks most suspicious. Ranking by cumulative time decides where to start.

questions.prompt: After fixing one stage, what does Procedure 57.2 say to re-measure?
options: Only the stage that was fixed, to confirm the fix
The next stage only, since it is now the bottleneck
Nothing, if the fix followed a known chapter's advice
The whole pipeline, not just the stage you fixed
questions.explanation: Fixing one stage can shift where time goes. Re-measuring everything shows the new ranking before the next fix.

questions.prompt: Which stage dominated the naive pipeline?
options: All three took about the same time
Loading the CSV with csv.reader, at about 216 ms
Model scoring, one row at a time, at about 8 s
The watchlist check against a list, at about 773 ms
questions.explanation: Scoring took 8,052 ms of the 9,041 ms total. Loading and feature engineering together were about 1 s.

questions.prompt: Which fix did the capstone apply to the watchlist check?
options: Reading the watchlist with mmap
Moving the list scan to the GPU
.isin(set) with vectorised string operations
Running the list scan in a process pool of 16 workers
questions.explanation: A set makes membership O(1) (Chapter 51), and vectorised operations remove per-row Python work (Chapter 52). The stage went from 773.2 ms to 381.9 ms.

refLinks.label: §57.2.2 Fixing Each Stage With the Chapter That Predicts the Fix

questions.prompt: The three CPU-side fixes cut the pipeline from 9,040.8 ms to 725.2 ms. What is the overall speedup? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 9,040.8 / 725.2 = 12.47, about 12.5x, before the GPU was considered.

questions.prompt: Where did the biggest single win, 34.7x, come from?
options: Replacing csv.reader with pandas.read_csv
Moving scoring to the GPU
Using a set for the watchlist check
One batched forward pass for scoring
questions.explanation: Batching removed Python per-row overhead entirely, with no hardware change. That is Chapter 53's amortisation idea applied through batching.

refLinks.label: §57.2.2 Fixing Each Stage With the Chapter That Predicts the Fix

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter say the GPU question is only worth asking after the CPU fixes?
options: The CPU fixes made the data small enough to fit in GPU memory.
The GPU can't run code that hasn't been vectorised.
GPUs are always slower than CPUs on tabular data.
Cheap CPU fixes removed most of the time first, for less effort.
questions.explanation: 12.5x came before any hardware change. Checking GPU offload first could have credited the GPU with a win that batching alone delivered.

refLinks.label: §57.2.2 Fixing Each Stage With the Chapter That Predicts the Fix

questions.prompt: The first GPU scoring call took 443.9 ms, slower than the CPU's 232.1 ms. Why isn't that a real result?
options: The GPU was still computing the previous batch.
The CPU result was measured with the wrong clock.
It includes one-time CUDA context initialisation.
The model ran in double precision on its first call.
questions.explanation: The first CUDA call in a process pays setup costs. Warm, the same call took 3.7 ms of wall time.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter say is the real lesson of the cold-start trap appearing again?
options: GPUs are unreliable for benchmarking and should be avoided.
The warm-up rule only matters for very large models.
The warm-up step must be done every time, not just known.
Cold-start numbers are the true cost, since users hit them.
questions.explanation: The trap had been taught twice already and still nearly produced a wrong conclusion. The step has to be executed, not just remembered.

refLinks.label: §57.2.3 The GPU Question, and the Same Trap One More Time

questions.prompt: The warm GPU scoring took 3.7 ms of wall time against 232.1 ms batched on the CPU. What speedup do these figures give? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: 232.1 / 3.7 = 62.7, about 63x. The book reports 62.1x from unrounded timings.

questions.prompt: Scoring 2,000 rows one call at a time used 12.740 ms of GPU time. One batched call used 0.045 ms. How many times less GPU time did batching use? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: 12.740 / 0.045 = 283, for identical output, with 10,000 kernel launches against 6.

questions.prompt: What does the nsys comparison show was wrong with the naive GPU use?
options: The PCIe link, which ran at a lower generation than expected
The number of times the GPU was invoked, not the GPU itself
The GPU's clock speed, which was throttled during the run
The matmul algorithm, which was the wrong one for the GPU
questions.explanation: Thousands of tiny launches carry fixed overhead each. One batched launch amortises it, the same idea as pool reuse and chunk sizing.

refLinks.label: §57.2.4 Confirming the Real Fix Is Batching, Not “the GPU”

questions.prompt: The full pipeline with warm GPU scoring took 496.8 ms against 9,040.8 ms naive. What is the overall speedup? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 9,040.8 / 496.8 = 18.2x. The CPU fixes alone had already delivered 12.5x of it.

questions.prompt: A team plans to move a slow scoring stage to a GPU instance. It scores rows one at a time in a Python loop. What does the capstone suggest doing first?
options: Parallelise the row loop across processes, then move to the GPU.
Move it to the GPU at once, since scoring is a matmul and GPUs win on matmuls.
Batch it on the current machine first, then benchmark the GPU warm.
Benchmark the GPU on its first call after deploy, since users will hit that.
questions.explanation: The capstone's 34.7x came from batching with no new hardware. A cold first call looked 0.52x and would have pointed the wrong way.

bookExercises.prompt: State Procedure 57.1's rule about the first step of any performance investigation, and name the tool this chapter uses to follow it.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Never guess which fix to apply. Profile first, always. This chapter uses `cProfile` (on a representative subset) to rank stages by cumulative time before touching any code.

bookExercises.prompt: List the three CPU-side fixes applied in this chapter's Worked Example (load, feature engineering, scoring) and state which chapter's finding predicted each one.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Load: `csv.reader` → `pandas.read_csv`, predicted by the Memory & I/O Optimization chapter's "let a C parser do the IO" finding. Feature engineering: list-scan → `.isin(set)` + vectorized string ops, predicted by the Algorithmic & Data Structure Optimization chapter's set-vs-list finding and the Vectorization & SIMD chapter's vectorization finding. Model scoring: row-at-a-time → one batched forward pass, predicted by the Parallelism on CPU chapter's overhead-amortisation principle, applied here via batching rather than multiprocessing.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's measured cold-start result (443.9ms, GPU looking 0.52x, slower than CPU) versus the warm result (3.7ms wall, 62.1x faster than CPU), compute how many times larger the cold-start measurement is than the warm one, and explain what this ratio represents physically.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `443.9 / 3.7 ≈ 120x` larger (wall-clock comparison); using the pure-compute figure, `443.9 / 1.923 ≈ 231x` larger. This ratio represents the one-time CUDA context initialisation cost. Nearly all of the 443.9ms cold measurement is process/context setup that only happens once per process, not per-call compute. The warm measurement isolates the actual matmul cost, which the cold measurement almost entirely obscures.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the final Nsight comparison's measured numbers (12.740ms across 10,000 kernel launches for individual calls vs. 0.045ms across 6 kernel launches for one batched call), explain why "283x less actual GPU-side time for identical output" is stronger evidence that batching (not "the GPU") was the real fix than the wall-clock comparison alone would have been.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The wall-clock comparison alone (232.1ms CPU-batched vs. 3.7ms warm GPU) already shows GPU winning, but it doesn't by itself prove *why*. It's consistent with either "the GPU computes faster" or "the GPU computes about the same but something else changed." The Nsight comparison isolates the actual mechanism: identical output, but 10,000 kernel launches at 12.740ms of real GPU-side time for individual calls versus 6 kernel launches at 0.045ms for one batched call, proving directly, via real launch counts and measured GPU-side time (not wall-clock, which includes CPU-side dispatch overhead too), that the difference is specifically the *number of GPU invocations*, not a difference in how fast the GPU computes per call. This distinguishes "batching helped" from "the GPU is just fast," which the wall-clock number alone cannot.

bookExercises.prompt: A team concludes "GPU scoring is slower than CPU for our model" after measuring their first-ever call to a newly loaded GPU model at 400ms against a 230ms CPU baseline. Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say before accepting that conclusion.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Before accepting that conclusion, check whether that 400ms first-call measurement included the model's first-ever CUDA call in the process. This chapter's own Worked Example showed an identical trap producing a 0.52x 'GPU is slower' result that reversed to a genuine 62.1x GPU win once the cold-start cost was excluded and the call was repeated warm. A single un-warmed GPU measurement compared against an already-warm CPU baseline isn't a fair comparison, and it's very likely CUDA context initialisation being mistaken for model latency."

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter's overall CPU-only speedup (12.5x) and GPU-inclusive speedup (18.2x) are both reported relative to the naive 9,040.8ms baseline. Explain why reporting the GPU speedup relative to the CPU-optimised version (232.1ms → 3.7ms, i.e. within-stage) AND relative to the naive baseline (9,040.8ms → 496.8ms, i.e. end-to-end) are both meaningful numbers that answer different questions.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The within-stage number (232.1ms → 3.7ms, 62.1x) answers "how much does GPU batching help the scoring step specifically, once everything else is already optimised," useful for deciding whether GPU offload is worth the added deployment complexity for that one stage. The end-to-end number (9,040.8ms → 496.8ms, 18.2x) answers "how much did the whole investigation improve total pipeline time," the number a stakeholder actually experiences and the one that matters for a go/no-go decision on the whole project. Both are legitimate and answer genuinely different questions. Reporting only the larger, more impressive-sounding one without the other would obscure which fixes (CPU-side batching, 12.5x of the total) versus GPU offload (the remaining increment to 18.2x) actually did the work.

bookExercises.prompt: Read Gregg's USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) referenced in "Systems Performance." Explain how this chapter's GPU utilisation measurement (from the prior chapter's `nsys`-based technique) maps onto the "Utilization" component of the USE method, and what the "Saturation" component would add that raw utilisation alone doesn't capture.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: GPU utilisation (from the prior chapter's `nsys`-based measurement, the fraction of wall-clock time the GPU is actually busy) maps directly onto USE's "Utilization" component: it answers "how much of the available time was this resource doing work." "Saturation" would add a different question the raw utilisation number can't answer on its own: whether work is queuing up *waiting* for the resource even when it isn't at 100% utilisation, e.g., whether requests are backing up in a queue for GPU time even at, say, 40% utilisation, which would indicate a scheduling or batching problem distinct from "the GPU isn't busy enough." Utilisation alone, as this book's prior chapter showed, can be low (under 1%) with no saturation at all. The GPU simply isn't given enough work per call, a different diagnosis than a saturated, queued-up resource would imply.
